notes.text: Ziklag — Which though burnt, yet was not so consumed by the fire, that David and his men could not lodge in it.

Judah — These he more particularly teacheth, because they were the chief, and now the royal tribe, and likely to be the great bulwark to all Israel against the Philistines, upon whose land they bordered; and withal, to be the most true to him, and to his interest. The bow - That is, of their arms, expressed, under the name of the bow, which then was one of the chief weapons; and for the dextrous use whereof Jonathan is commended in the following song: which may be one reason, why he now gives forth this order, that so they might strive to imitate Jonathan in military skill, and to excel in it, as he did. Jasher - It is more largely and particularly described in the book of Jasher.

Beauty — Their flower and glory. Saul and Jonathan, and their army. High places - Hebrew. upon thy high places; that is, those which belong to thee, O land of Israel. How - How strangely! How suddenly! How universally!

Tell it not — This is not a precept, but a poetical wish; whereby he doth not so much desire, that this might not be done, which he knew to be impossible; as, express his great sorrow, because it would be done, to the dishonour of God, and of his people. The daughters - He mentions these, because it was the custom of women in those times and places to celebrate those victories which their men obtained, with triumphant songs and dances.

Let there be, &c. — This is no proper imprecation; but a passionate representation of the horror which he conceived at this publick loss; which was such, as if he thought every person or thing which contributed to it, were fit to bear the tokens of divine displeasure, such as this is, when the earth wants the necessary influences of dew and rain. Fields of offerings - That is, fruitful fields, which may produce fair and goodly fruits fit to be offered to God. Vilely - Dishonourably: for it was a great reproach to any soldier, to cast away or lose his shield. Cast away - By themselves, that they might flee more swiftly as the Israelites did, and Saul with the rest. As though, &c. - As if he had been no more, than a common soldier: he was exposed to the same kind of death and reproach as they were.

Not back — Without effect: their arrows shot from their bow, and their swords did seldom miss, and commonly pierced fat, and flesh, and blood, and reached even to the heart and bowels. Returned not, &c. - But filled and glutted with blood: for the sword is metaphorically said to have a mouth, which we translate an edge; and to devour. And this their former successfulness is mentioned as an aggravation of their last infelicity.

Lovely — Amiable, and obliging in their carriage and conversation, both towards one another, and towards their people: for, as for Saul's fierce behaviour towards Jonathan, it was only a sudden passion, by which his ordinary temper was not to be measured; and for his carriage towards David, that was from that jealousy and reason of state which usually engageth even well- natured princes, to the same hostilities. But it is observable, that David speaks not a word here of his piety; but only commends him for those things which were truly in him. A fit pattern for all preachers in their funeral commendations. Swifter, &c. - Expeditious in pursuing their enemies, and executing their designs; which is a great commendation in a prince, and in a soldier. Stronger, &c. - In regard of their bodily strength, and the courage of their mind.

Daughters — These he mentions; because the women then used to make songs both of triumph, and of lamentation, and, because they usually are most delighted with the ornaments of the body here following. Clothed you - This he did, because he procured them so much peace as gave them opportunity of enriching themselves: and, because he took these things as spoils from the enemies, and clothed his own people with them.
Thine — Which were in thy country, and (had not thy father disinherited thee by his sins) in thy dominions.

Distressed — That is, for the loss of thee. For, besides the loss of a true friend, which is inestimable; he lost him who both could, and undoubtedly would have given him a speedy, and quiet, and sure possession of the kingdom, whereas now, he met with long and troublesome interruptions. Of women - That is, that love wherewith they love their husbands, or children for their affections are usually more ardent than mens. David goes up to Hebron and is crowned there, ver. 1-4. Thanks the men of Jabesh-gilead, ver. 5-7. Ishbosheth is set up in opposition to him, ver. 8-11. An encounter between David's men and Ishbosheth's, in which the latter are beaten, ver. 12-17. Asahel is killed by Abner, ver. 18-23. Joah sounds retreat by the advice of Abner, who retires to Mahanaim, ver. 24-29. The loss on each side, ver. 30-31. Asahel buried, ver. 32

glossa.text:
*The sons.* The sons of Juda, sons of confession, whom the true David wills to be fortified with the bow of Scripture, lest through ignorance they fall down in the sight of the demons.

*The bow. ((RAB. in lib. Reg.))* Because the Philisthiim are archers, by which art they had killed Saul, he wills them to learn that same art of war, or he commanded that the kings of Juda should teach fortitude, that is, that they should be strong and intent in the fear of the Lord, lest they perish as Saul did.

*In the book. ((RAB., ubi supra.)) It is read,* or, *it is written.* They assert that this book is nowhere to be found, like the book of the wars of the Lord, etc., *as far as* how Saul, drawing back from the fear of the Lord, perished through obedience *obedientiam*; read *inobedientiam*, "disobedience".

*Consider, Israel.* ((ID.)) Thou who hast remained, for what fault they were slain, and beware lest thou too perish in their wickedness.

*Geth.* A winepress, that is, Jerusalem, which killeth the prophets ((Matth. XXIII)), to whom the death of the Lord and of the apostles was a matter of mockery, and for this cause the true David commanded that his passion should not be announced to them.

*The mountains of Gelboe,* etc. ((ID.)) Others, high places, because, that is, O Saul, thy disobedience was accounted as idolatry in the high places, since it is the wickedness of idolatry to be unwilling to acquiesce. The mountains of Gelboe were most rich before the curse, and they say that even until now they lie under the curse, and they testify that it never rains there.

David, king and prophet, who did not render evils to his persecutors, when Saul and Jonathas had fallen in battle, in his lamentation curses the mountains of Gelboe: *Ye mountains of Gelboe, neither dew,* etc., *as far as* and the divine power fulfilled the sentence of him who cursed. And so for the spectacle of the king's slaying the elements paid the penalty.

((RAB.)) What have the mountains done amiss? etc., *as far as* they who had deserved, iniquity requiring it, to receive the death of their king among themselves.

*From the blood of the slain.* Blood and fat furnish strength to the body, so those men gave fortitude to their subjects, by whom Saul and Jonathas were slain as though not by rustics. Or thus, Saul was reprobated by God, and slain basely by the uncircumcised, as though he had not been anointed with oil, because of the blood of the slain, that is, of the seventy-five priests who burned fat to the Lord, whom Saul commanded to be slain though they were harmless.

*The arrow.* It signifies that Jonathan and Saul were warlike and most valiant, and it praises in them the comeliness of form and the constancy of mind.

((RAB.)) Allegorically. The holy prophet David figuratively bewails Saul and Jonathan, etc., *as far as* lest, being again shamefully overcome, they give joy to their enemies.

notes.text: Mark — Observe them accurately and punish them as they deserve. Stand - At thy tribunal.

Forgiveness — Thou art able and ready to forgive repenting sinners. Feared - Not with a slavish, but with a childlike fear. This mercy of thine is the foundation of all religion, without which men would desperately proceed in their impious courses.
I wait — That he would pardon my sins.
They — Whether soldiers that keep the night-watches in an army, or the priests or Levites who did so in the temple.

Israel — Every true Israelite. Plenteous - Abundantly sufficient for all persons who accept it upon God's terms. David testifies his humility, and exhorts Israel to trust in God, ver. 1-3. A song of degrees of David.

glossa.text:
*A canticle of degrees.* ((ID.)) The eleventh degree, etc., *as far as* a glad conclusion is set down with the certainty of pardon, there, *Let Israel hope in the Lord.*

*Out of the depths.* ((AUG.)) He who feels himself in the deep, etc., *as far as* as the Scripture says: *The sinner, when he shall have come into the depth of vices, contemneth.*

*Who shall abide it.* ((ID.)) Because well nigh all human life is barked at round about by sins, and every conscience is accused by its own thoughts. That heart is not chaste which presumes upon its own justice. Let it therefore presume upon the mercy of God, *For with him there is propitiation,* whence he subjoins:

*For with thee there is propitiation.* As it were: In what hope dost thou cry? Because there is mercy in thee, wherefore he speaks thus: Or join it thus.

((AUG.)) No man can abide it, etc., *as far as* one hope therefore there is: *For with thee there is propitiation,* etc., *For thy law's sake,* ((ID.)) I have waited for the *law* of mercy, etc., *as far as* and thou hast given this law in the very necessity.

*The morning.* ((ID.)) Let him hope in the morning watch who hopes for nothing else from God than immortality. *From the morning watch,* etc., *as far as* thence in the law the head and the tail of the victim were offered to the Lord. *Let Israel hope in the Lord.* ((CASS.)) The second part, where is the glad conclusion: Secure concerning himself, he preaches that they should hope always in the Lord. As it were, as his soul has hoped, so let Israel hope.
*And he shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities.* ((ID.)) Here he has now said what that one shall do, whom he called merciful and plentiful.

notes.text: For ye know — And this knowledge is the true source of love. The grace - The most sincere, most free, and most abundant love. He became poor - In becoming man, in all his life; in his death. Rich - In the favour and image of God.

A man — Every believer. Is accepted - With God. According to what he hath - And the same rule holds universally. Whoever acknowledges himself to be a vile, guilty sinner, and, in consequence of this acknowledgment, flies for refuge to the wounds of a crucified saviour, and relies on his merits alone for salvation, may in every circumstance of life apply this indulgent declaration to himself.

That their abundance — If need should so require. May be - At another time. A supply to your want: that there may be an equality - No want on one side, no superfluity on the other. It may likewise have a further meaning:-that as the temporal bounty of the Corinthians did now supply the temporal wants of their poor brethren in Judea, so the prayers of these might be a means of bringing down many spiritual blessings on their benefactors: so that all the spiritual wants of the one might be amply supplied; all the temporal of the other.
As it is written, He that had gathered the most had nothing over; and he that had gathered the least did not lack — That is, in which that scripture is in another sense fulfilled. Exod. xvi, 18

glossa.text: *Not as commanding,* etc. Not only did I ask Titus, but I myself say that you should abound, *not as commanding.* That is, not as enjoining a penance, because so the Corinthians would be held as by a vow.

*He became needy.* He does not say, he became poor, when he had been rich: but, *when he was rich.* For he took up poverty, and did not lose his riches: within rich, without poor; God lying hidden in riches, man appearing in poverty.

*That by poverty for him.* For through his poverty we cast off abjicicimus the rags of iniquity, that we may be clothed with the robe of immortality. All therefore have been made rich, believing in the poor Christ. Let no man therefore despise himself, poor in his cell, rich in conscience. He sleeps more securely on the ground than the man rich in gold in his purple. Be not therefore afraid to come with thy beggary to him who, clothed with our poverty, where he made himself poor, made us rich.
*But also to will.* As if to say: Some of you had willed it, but some had begun it: now, however, let both accomplish it.
*But by equality.* Let each one divide with the saints as much as he has, because no more is required than he ought to keep for himself: so Zacchaeus gave the half of his goods to the poor.

*That there may be an equality.* Not but that they differ in brightness: but because to all it is the same, and to all there will be sufficiency. *As it is written.* Of the manna, as a sign of this thing.

*He that had much did not abound.* The saints have more in the hope of what is to come, less those who are rich in time, and yet there they shall be made equal. So that as here they support the want of the saints, so there they may be supported by them, and shall become rich in the eternal good. *He that had much did not abound.* So the rich man who gives much, and the poor man who gives little, if the will of both be equal, have an equal reward.

notes.text: Luke viii, 40.

One of the rulers of the synagogue — To regulate the affairs of every synagogue, there was a council of grave men. Over these was a president, who was termed the ruler of the synagogue. Sometimes there was no more than one ruler in a synagogue. Matt. ix, 18; Luke viii, 41.
Matt. ix, 20; Luke viii, 43.
John, the brother of James — When St. Mark wrote, not long after our Lord's ascension, the memory of St. James, lately beheaded, was so fresh, that his name was more known than that of John himself.
Them that were with him — Peter, James, and John.

He charged them that no man should know it — That he might avoid every appearance of vain glory, might prevent too great a concourse of people, and might not further enrage the scribes and Pharisees against him; the time for his death, and for the full manifestation of his glory, being not yet come. He commanded something should be given her to eat - So that when either natural or spiritual life is restored, even by immediate miracle, all proper means are to be used in order to preserve it.

glossa.text:
*And there cometh a certain man,* etc. ((HIER.)) After these things Jairus the ruler of the synagogue comes, because when the fulness of the Gentiles shall have entered in, then all Israel, etc., *as far as* Abraham and Moses and Samuel pray for the dead people, and Jesus follows their prayers.

((BEDA.)) Jairus, *enlightening* or *enlightened:* because he enlightened the people with the words of life: and that he might be able to do this, he was enlightened by the Holy Ghost.

*For my daughter. ((BEDA.))* Luke: *For he had one only daughter, about twelve years old, and she was dying ((Luc. VIII))*. The daughter of the ruler of the synagogue is the Synagogue, by the legal institution alone, etc., *as far as* suddenly laid low by the languor of errors, she despairingly forsook the spiritual ways.

*And they thronged him.* While he goes to heal the girl, he is thronged by the crowd: because, offering to the Jews the warnings of salvation by which he might raise up their sick conscience, he was burdened by the harmful custom of carnal peoples.

*And a woman,* etc. As the Lord goes on toward the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, the diseased woman of twelve years snatches health before her, and afterwards the daughter was healed and was raised up: because the salvation of the human race was so dispensed that first some out of Israel, then the fulness of the Gentiles, and so all Israel shall be saved.

((BEDA.)) It is to be noted that the girl was twelve years old and that the woman flowed with blood twelve years, etc., *as far as* while Christ was determining to heal Judaea, she forestalled with sure hope the salvation already prepared and promised to others.

*Having suffered many things,* etc. ((ID.)) From false theologians, philosophers, teachers of the secular laws, who promised that they would give useful precepts of living. The demons too, etc., *as far as* they began both to hope for and to seek out a remedy for their languor.

*She came in the crowd. ((ID.)) If any man minister to me, let him follow me ((Joan. XII))*. And elsewhere: *Thou shalt walk after the Lord God ((Ose. XI))*. Or because she does not see God present in the flesh, but afterwards comes to the grace of the acknowledgment of faith, etc., *as far as* by the evangelical sacraments, as by his own garments, he cleanses the fountains of unclean blood.

*Who touched me. ((BEDA.))* The faithful woman alone touches the Lord, whom the crowd accompanying him on every side throngs. Because he, who is burdened by the diverse heresies of them that disorderly throng together, or by perverse manners, is touched only by the faithful heart of the Church; whence: *Touch me not: for I am not yet ascended to my Father ((Joan. XX))*. Because to touch him truly is to believe him equal to the Father.

 ((HIER.)) By the seventh virtue the dead girl is raised, but on the way the woman with the issue of blood touches the hem from behind, who together with health her substance, etc., *as far as* the cymbal, confession; the pomegranate signifies the will of martyrdom and the whiteness of the virtues.

*But the woman. ((BEDA.))* Behold whither the questioning tended, namely, that the woman should confess the truth of her long infirmity, and of her sudden believing and healing: and that so she herself might be confirmed in faith and might afford an example to others.

*While he was yet,* etc. ((BEDA.)) The woman being healed, straightway the girl is announced dead: because the Church of the Gentiles, cured of the stain of vices, and for the merit of her faith, etc., *as far as* but what is impossible to men is possible to God.

*To the ruler of the synagogue.* The ruler of the synagogue is the company of the teachers of the law, of whom: *Upon the chair of Moses have sitten the scribes and the Pharisees ((Matth. XXVIII))*. And if they shall be willing to believe, the Synagogue also that is subject to them shall be saved.

*And he admitted not,* etc. ((BEDA.)) The mysteries are not to be revealed to blasphemers and mockers, but to the faithful who may honour them. Whence elsewhere: *Wisdom is justified by all her children ((Matth. XI))*.

*Weeping and wailing. (ID)*. *Let all rejoice that hope in the Lord, and they shall exult for ever, and thou shalt dwell in them ((Psal. V))*. This gladness the Synagogue lost by the desert of her unbelief: and therefore she lies dead among those that weep and howl. But Jesus does not suffer her to perish utterly.

*She is not dead.* To me, in whose disposing both the soul that has been received lives and the flesh that is to be raised rests. Hence it is a custom among Christians that the dead, who are not doubted to be about to rise again, are called sleepers; whence: *We will not have you ignorant, brethren, concerning them that sleep ((I Thess. IV))*.

((BEDA.)) Since the soul that shall have sinned dies, yet that soul which the Lord foresees unto eternal life may not unfittingly be said to have been dead indeed to us, but to have fallen asleep to him.

*All being cast out. ((ID.))* The crowd is cast out that the girl may be raised: because unless the multitude of secular cares be cast out from the heart, the soul that lies dead within is not raised. For while it scatters itself through all its thoughts, it in no wise gathers itself to the consideration of itself.

*Talitha cumi.* In the Syriac speech which the evangelist sets down it is no more than: Girl, arise. But perhaps to express the force of the Lord's command he added this: *I say to thee, arise,* and took care to convey the sense of the speaker rather than his words. So often the apostles and the evangelists, when they take up some testimony, set down the sense rather than the words.

((HIER.)) To the girl it is said *Talitha cumi,* that is, Girl, arise. To the ruler of the synagogue, etc., *as far as* whence it is said: *Abraham believed God, and it was reputed to him unto justice ((Jac. II))*.

((BEDA.)) That Christ raised three dead persons signifies three kinds of souls. He raises the girl, etc., *as far as* he heard of a fourth dead man when a disciple announced it: but because living men to pray for him were wanting: *Let,* he says, *the dead bury their dead ((Matth. VIII))*.

Out of the depths I cry to you

Pass Me Not, O Gentle Savior

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: If a poor man, one of your brothers, is with you within any of your gates in your land which Yahweh your God gives you, you shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand from your poor brother; but you shall surely open your hand to him, and shall surely lend him sufficient for his need, which he lacks. Beware that there not be a base thought in your heart, saying, “The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand”; and your eye be evil against your […]
echoes.note: Paul's appeal that the Macedonians gave generously out of deep poverty rests on the Deuteronomic open-hand command: do not harden your heart against the poor brother but give freely. The 'fellowship in service to the saints' (v.4) reflects the same covenantal obligation to relieve a needy member of God's people. Coherence with the whole collection theme is high, though the verbal link is thematic rather than lexical.

echoes.text: There is one who scatters, and increases yet more. There is one who withholds more than is appropriate, but gains poverty. The liberal soul shall be made fat. He who waters shall be watered also himself.
echoes.note: The paradox that the Macedonians' deep poverty 'abounded to the riches of their liberality' (v.2) echoes the wisdom maxim that one who scatters yet increases and the liberal soul is made rich. The generosity-brings-abundance reversal is a recurring sapiential theme Paul draws on through the chapter; volume is modest, coherence strong.

echoes.text: ‘Take from among you an offering to Yahweh. Whoever is of a willing heart, let him bring it, Yahweh’s offering: gold, silver, brass,
echoes.note: The Macedonians giving 'of their own accord' and begging to share in the collection (vv.3-4) recalls the willing-hearted offering for the tabernacle, where everyone whose heart stirred him brought a freewill gift. The collection-for-the-sanctuary typology underlies Paul's framing of the Jerusalem fund as a sacred offering. Faint and contested as a deliberate echo.

echoes.text: He who has a generous eye will be blessed; for he shares his food with the poor.
echoes.note: The summons to a willing readiness in giving 'according to what you have' (vv.11-12) resonates with the blessing on the bountiful eye that gives bread to the poor. The wisdom tradition that values the disposition of the giver over the amount stands behind Paul's stress on willingness; the link is thematic and faint.

echoes.text: For he grew up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of dry ground. He has no good looks or majesty. When we see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him. He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him. Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and […]
echoes.note: The Christological reversal in v.9, 'though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor,' may evoke the Servant who, despised and stripped of form, is poured out and yet by his abasement enriches the many. The pattern of voluntary self-impoverishment for others' gain coheres with Isaiah's Servant, but the conceptual frame of pre-existent riches is Pauline rather than verbal Isaianic; contested.

echoes.text: When they measured it with an omer, he who gathered much had nothing over, and he who gathered little had no lack. They gathered every man according to his eating.
echoes.note: Verse 15 explicitly quotes ('as it is written') the manna narrative: 'He who gathered much had nothing left over, and he who gathered little had no lack.' Paul lifts the LXX wording of the equalizing of the manna to ground his principle of economic equality among the assemblies. Volume, explicit citation formula, and coherence with the equality theme are all maximal.

echoes.text: “‘If your brother has become poor, and his hand can’t support himself among you; then you shall uphold him. He shall live with you like an alien and a temporary resident. Take no interest from him or profit, but fear your God; that your brother may live among you. You shall not lend him your money at interest, nor give him your food for profit.
echoes.note: The principle of 'equality' so that one's abundance supplies another's lack (vv.13-14) resonates with the Jubilee/sabbatical ethic of sustaining the impoverished brother without profit. The leveling vision behind Paul's mutual-supply argument is at home in the Holiness Code's economy of need; faint and thematic.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: “‘If a woman has a discharge of her blood many days not in the time of her period, or if she has a discharge beyond the time of her period; all the days of the discharge of her uncleanness shall be as in the days of her period: she is unclean. Every bed whereon she lies all the days of her discharge shall be to her as the bed of her period: and everything whereon she sits shall be unclean, as the uncleanness of her period. Whoever touches these things […]
echoes.note: The woman 'with an issue of blood' (v.25) embodies the Levitical zavah: a woman with a discharge beyond her period is unclean all the days of the flow, and whatever and whoever she touches becomes unclean. Her touching Jesus' garment (v.27) inverts the expected contagion — purity flows outward rather than impurity inward. Very high Volume and Thematic Coherence; the legal background is essential to the scene's meaning.

echoes.text: “‘If a woman has a discharge, and her discharge in her flesh is blood, she shall be in her impurity seven days: and whoever touches her shall be unclean until the evening.
echoes.note: The baseline menstrual-impurity law ('seven days she shall be in her impurity, and whoever touches her shall be unclean') frames the chronic twelve-year condition (v.25). Establishes that the woman is perpetually outside normal social and cultic contact, deepening the audacity of her approach in the crowd.

echoes.text: The priest shall offer the one for a sin offering, and the other for a burnt offering; and the priest shall make atonement for her before Yahweh for the uncleanness of her discharge.
echoes.note: The law's resolution requires the priest to make atonement 'for her unclean discharge,' after which she is clean. Jesus' word 'be cured of your disease' (v.34) functions as the priestly declaration of restored cleanness, the discharge being 'dried up' (v.29). Thematic coherence: Jesus enacts the role the Levitical system assigns to atonement and priestly verdict.

echoes.text: But to you who fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in its wings. You will go out, and leap like calves of the stall.
echoes.note: 'The sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings (kanaph)' — the same term denotes the hem/corner of a garment. The woman seeks healing by touching the edge of Jesus' clothes (vv.27-28), and Matthew/Luke specify the kraspedon (tassel). Faint but evocative: healing located in the garment's edge resonates with Malachi's healing 'in the wings.'

echoes.text: “Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them that they should make themselves fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations, and that they put on the fringe of each border a cord of blue: and it shall be to you for a fringe, that you may look on it, and remember all the commandments of Yahweh, and do them; and that you not follow after your own heart and your own eyes, after which you use to play the prostitute;
echoes.note: The command to wear tassels on the corners of garments as reminders of the commandments stands behind the Synoptic detail of touching the hem (here generalized as 'his clothes,' v.27). The healing power located in the garment's fringe gains resonance from the sanctity Torah attaches to the tassel; faint in Mark, who omits the tassel itself.

echoes.text: As they were burying a man, behold, they saw a band of raiders; and they threw the man into Elisha’s tomb. As soon as the man touched the bones of Elisha, he revived, and stood up on his feet.
echoes.note: Contact with Elisha's bones revives a corpse — power transmitted by touch from a holy person even involuntarily. The woman's cure by touching Jesus' garment, with power 'gone out from him' (v.30), echoes the prophetic motif of healing virtue conveyed through physical contact. Thematic, supporting the Elijah-Elisha typology that pervades the chapter.

echoes.text: After these things, the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, fell sick; and his sickness was so severe, that there was no breath left in him. She said to Elijah, “What have I to do with you, you man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to memory, and to kill my son!” He said to her, “Give me your son.” He took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into the room where he stayed, and laid him on his own bed. He cried to Yahweh, and said, […]
echoes.note: Elijah raises the widow of Zarephath's son: he goes in to where the child lies, acts privately, and 'the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived,' then Elijah presents the living child. Mark's raising of Jairus' daughter — entering where the child lay (v.40), the restoring word, the return to life (v.42) — is patterned on this paradigmatic prophetic resurrection. Strong Volume and recurrence within the chapter's Elijah-Elisha typology.

echoes.text: When Elisha had come into the house, behold, the child was dead, and laid on his bed. He went in therefore, and shut the door on them both, and prayed to Yahweh. He went up, and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the flesh of the child grew warm. Then he returned, and walked in the house once back and forth; and went up, and stretched himself on him. Then […]
echoes.note: Elisha raises the Shunammite's son: he enters alone with the dead child, shuts the door (cf. Jesus putting out the mourners, v.40), and the child revives; the mother falls at his feet (cf. Jairus, v.22). The closest single template for Jairus' daughter — privacy, exclusion of others, parental supplication, and bodily resurrection of a child — making the Elisha narrative a primary subtext.

echoes.text: He went up, and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the flesh of the child grew warm. Then he returned, and walked in the house once back and forth; and went up, and stretched himself on him. Then the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes.
echoes.note: Elisha's bodily, hands-on revival ('he put his mouth on his mouth... the flesh of the child grew warm') resonates with Jesus 'taking the child by the hand' (v.41). The motif of resurrection effected by the prophet's physical contact strengthens the Elisha typology beyond the structural parallels already noted in 4:32-37.

echoes.text: Elijah took the child, and brought him down out of the room into the house, and delivered him to his mother; and Elijah said, “Behold, your son lives.”
echoes.note: Elijah 'gave him to his mother' after the raising; Jesus likewise restores the child to her parents and orders that she be given food (v.43), confirming bodily life. The return-to-the-parent motif and the demonstration of real restored life cohere closely with the Elijah pattern.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: Jesus' euphemism 'the child is not dead, but is asleep' (v.39) trades on the OT/Second-Temple metaphor of death as sleep from which the dead awake, classically formulated in Daniel's 'many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake.' The raising functions as a proleptic sign of resurrection hope; thematic and verbal contact through the sleep-of-death idiom.

echoes.text: He said, “Swear to me,” and he swore to him. Israel bowed himself on the bed’s head.
echoes.note: Death-as-sleep language (e.g., the patriarchs 'sleeping with their fathers,' a recurrent OT idiom) underlies Jesus' 'she is asleep' (v.39), prompting the mourners' ridicule because they hear only literal sleep. Faint, depending on the broader idiom rather than a single text; cited to register the OT availability of the metaphor.

echoes.text: For his anger is but for a moment. His favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning.
echoes.note: 'Weeping may endure for a night, but joy comes in the morning' — the turning of mourning into rejoicing at a child's restoration loosely echoes the psalm's reversal from lament to deliverance, set against the 'weeping and great wailing' (v.38) Jesus overturns. Thematic only; included as a faint coherence with the chapter's reversal of death into life.

glossa.text: *For God.* That is, God is not the author of evils; for he created man unto immortality, who, consenting to the devil's suggestion, was made subject to the sentence of death.

notes.text: Cometh — Speedily and in due season.
Mountain — My kingdom: kingdoms are usually called mountains in prophetical writings.
Profit — What wilt thou gain by it? The dust - Shall they that are dead celebrate thy goodness in the land of the living? Or, shall my dust praise thee?

Sackcloth — Given me occasion to put off that sackcloth, which they used to wear in times of mourning, Esth iv, 1 chap. xxxv, 13 Isaiah xxxii, 11 Joel i, 13. Girded - With joy, as with a garment, surrounding me on every side.

My glory — My tongue. David professes his confidence in God, intermixing prayer to him, ver. 1-8. Complains to God and prays for deliverance, ver. 9-18. Concludes with giving glory to God, and encouraging others to trust him, ver. 19-24. To the chief musician, A psalm of David.

glossa.text: *O Lord my God, I have cried to thee,* etc. ((AUG.)) Christ, etc., *as far as* but not in the dedication.
*Into the pit.* ((HIER.)) That is, out of the pit of hell, where the souls of sinners are, lest, like them, I should fall headlong into death.
*Confess ye,* etc. ((AUG.)) Because out of his own goodness and holiness, not ours, he was mindful of us.

*For wrath.* ((ID.)) That is, vengeance, by which he avenged upon us the first sin, which by death you have loosed.

*At evening.* ((ID.)) Because wrath, etc., *as far as* that is, in the time of grace after the time before the law and under the law.

((HIER.)) *At evening.* Because, when the Lord had suffered and been buried, the Apostles and the women continued in weeping and groaning. *And in the morning gladness.* Because coming to the sepulchre in the morning they received from the Angels the glory of the resurrection. *Weeping.* ((CASS.)) It shall abide for men who look toward the evening, at which Adam turned aside and went out from paradise: but there shall be gladness for those who look toward the morning, at which Christ rose again.

*But I.* How he acted before the dedication and deserved it. ((AUG., CASS.)) He acts at evening. But I, while abundance was mine in paradise, said: I shall not be moved from this good, believing the devil who said: *Thou shalt not die the death ((Gen. III))* . But, O Lord, in *thy will thou hast given strength to my beauty;* which is, I was good and strong not of myself, but of thee. And that thou mightest show it: *Thou hast turned away thy face,* that is, thou hast sent me forth out of paradise: but now, set here, *I will cry to thee,* etc.

*Thou hast turned away.* ((CASS.)) God turned away his face from Christ, by exposing him to the passion and to death; and thus Christ was troubled: *My soul is sorrowful even unto death. ((Matth. XVI.)) Troubled.* ((AUG.)) Calling to mind that time of trouble and of misery, and set in it, I hear the voice of the head who is to die for me, saying: *To thee, O Lord, will I cry.*

*What profit is there in my blood.* ((ID.)) He shows the necessity by which he does not suffer him to go down into corruption. *Whilst I go down into corruption.* For if I do not rise again at once, and the body is corrupted, I shall announce to no one, I shall gain no one. Confession is twofold, let us never be without it: when it is ill with us in tribulations, let us confess our sins; when it is well, let us confess praise to God in the exultation of justice.
*The Lord hath heard.* ((CASS.)) He treats of how he received it, namely the dedication. He said: I will cry, I will beseech, but the Lord heard me beseeching.

*Thou hast cut my sackcloth.* ((ID.)) Sackcloth is a rough garment, granted for the use of labour or in a time of sadness, as to the Ninivites; that is, human flesh, which was rent by dying: and there came forth the corn of the glorious resurrection, or of the godhead. Or else, the penalty of sin, which being destroyed in the resurrection, the godhead before hidden was brought forth: just as what the sack conceals whole, it opens when rent. ((AUG.)) Sackcloth of goats or of kids is mortality, which Christ drew or took from sinners; whence: *Whilst they were troublesome to me, I was clothed with haircloth ((Psal. XXXIV))*, that they might not see what was within.
*I shall not be pricked.* ((ID.)) I shall not now die unto the end. *O Lord God, I will confess to thee for ever.* What is: *I will confess to thee for ever?* For ever I will praise thee.

notes.text: For ye know — And this knowledge is the true source of love. The grace - The most sincere, most free, and most abundant love. He became poor - In becoming man, in all his life; in his death. Rich - In the favour and image of God.

A man — Every believer. Is accepted - With God. According to what he hath - And the same rule holds universally. Whoever acknowledges himself to be a vile, guilty sinner, and, in consequence of this acknowledgment, flies for refuge to the wounds of a crucified saviour, and relies on his merits alone for salvation, may in every circumstance of life apply this indulgent declaration to himself.

That their abundance — If need should so require. May be - At another time. A supply to your want: that there may be an equality - No want on one side, no superfluity on the other. It may likewise have a further meaning:-that as the temporal bounty of the Corinthians did now supply the temporal wants of their poor brethren in Judea, so the prayers of these might be a means of bringing down many spiritual blessings on their benefactors: so that all the spiritual wants of the one might be amply supplied; all the temporal of the other.
As it is written, He that had gathered the most had nothing over; and he that had gathered the least did not lack — That is, in which that scripture is in another sense fulfilled. Exod. xvi, 18

glossa.text: *Not as commanding,* etc. Not only did I ask Titus, but I myself say that you should abound, *not as commanding.* That is, not as enjoining a penance, because so the Corinthians would be held as by a vow.

*He became needy.* He does not say, he became poor, when he had been rich: but, *when he was rich.* For he took up poverty, and did not lose his riches: within rich, without poor; God lying hidden in riches, man appearing in poverty.

*That by poverty for him.* For through his poverty we cast off abjicicimus the rags of iniquity, that we may be clothed with the robe of immortality. All therefore have been made rich, believing in the poor Christ. Let no man therefore despise himself, poor in his cell, rich in conscience. He sleeps more securely on the ground than the man rich in gold in his purple. Be not therefore afraid to come with thy beggary to him who, clothed with our poverty, where he made himself poor, made us rich.
*But also to will.* As if to say: Some of you had willed it, but some had begun it: now, however, let both accomplish it.
*But by equality.* Let each one divide with the saints as much as he has, because no more is required than he ought to keep for himself: so Zacchaeus gave the half of his goods to the poor.

*That there may be an equality.* Not but that they differ in brightness: but because to all it is the same, and to all there will be sufficiency. *As it is written.* Of the manna, as a sign of this thing.

*He that had much did not abound.* The saints have more in the hope of what is to come, less those who are rich in time, and yet there they shall be made equal. So that as here they support the want of the saints, so there they may be supported by them, and shall become rich in the eternal good. *He that had much did not abound.* So the rich man who gives much, and the poor man who gives little, if the will of both be equal, have an equal reward.

notes.text: Luke viii, 40.

One of the rulers of the synagogue — To regulate the affairs of every synagogue, there was a council of grave men. Over these was a president, who was termed the ruler of the synagogue. Sometimes there was no more than one ruler in a synagogue. Matt. ix, 18; Luke viii, 41.
Matt. ix, 20; Luke viii, 43.
John, the brother of James — When St. Mark wrote, not long after our Lord's ascension, the memory of St. James, lately beheaded, was so fresh, that his name was more known than that of John himself.
Them that were with him — Peter, James, and John.

He charged them that no man should know it — That he might avoid every appearance of vain glory, might prevent too great a concourse of people, and might not further enrage the scribes and Pharisees against him; the time for his death, and for the full manifestation of his glory, being not yet come. He commanded something should be given her to eat - So that when either natural or spiritual life is restored, even by immediate miracle, all proper means are to be used in order to preserve it.

glossa.text:
*And there cometh a certain man,* etc. ((HIER.)) After these things Jairus the ruler of the synagogue comes, because when the fulness of the Gentiles shall have entered in, then all Israel, etc., *as far as* Abraham and Moses and Samuel pray for the dead people, and Jesus follows their prayers.

((BEDA.)) Jairus, *enlightening* or *enlightened:* because he enlightened the people with the words of life: and that he might be able to do this, he was enlightened by the Holy Ghost.

*For my daughter. ((BEDA.))* Luke: *For he had one only daughter, about twelve years old, and she was dying ((Luc. VIII))*. The daughter of the ruler of the synagogue is the Synagogue, by the legal institution alone, etc., *as far as* suddenly laid low by the languor of errors, she despairingly forsook the spiritual ways.

*And they thronged him.* While he goes to heal the girl, he is thronged by the crowd: because, offering to the Jews the warnings of salvation by which he might raise up their sick conscience, he was burdened by the harmful custom of carnal peoples.

*And a woman,* etc. As the Lord goes on toward the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, the diseased woman of twelve years snatches health before her, and afterwards the daughter was healed and was raised up: because the salvation of the human race was so dispensed that first some out of Israel, then the fulness of the Gentiles, and so all Israel shall be saved.

((BEDA.)) It is to be noted that the girl was twelve years old and that the woman flowed with blood twelve years, etc., *as far as* while Christ was determining to heal Judaea, she forestalled with sure hope the salvation already prepared and promised to others.

*Having suffered many things,* etc. ((ID.)) From false theologians, philosophers, teachers of the secular laws, who promised that they would give useful precepts of living. The demons too, etc., *as far as* they began both to hope for and to seek out a remedy for their languor.

*She came in the crowd. ((ID.)) If any man minister to me, let him follow me ((Joan. XII))*. And elsewhere: *Thou shalt walk after the Lord God ((Ose. XI))*. Or because she does not see God present in the flesh, but afterwards comes to the grace of the acknowledgment of faith, etc., *as far as* by the evangelical sacraments, as by his own garments, he cleanses the fountains of unclean blood.

*Who touched me. ((BEDA.))* The faithful woman alone touches the Lord, whom the crowd accompanying him on every side throngs. Because he, who is burdened by the diverse heresies of them that disorderly throng together, or by perverse manners, is touched only by the faithful heart of the Church; whence: *Touch me not: for I am not yet ascended to my Father ((Joan. XX))*. Because to touch him truly is to believe him equal to the Father.

 ((HIER.)) By the seventh virtue the dead girl is raised, but on the way the woman with the issue of blood touches the hem from behind, who together with health her substance, etc., *as far as* the cymbal, confession; the pomegranate signifies the will of martyrdom and the whiteness of the virtues.

*But the woman. ((BEDA.))* Behold whither the questioning tended, namely, that the woman should confess the truth of her long infirmity, and of her sudden believing and healing: and that so she herself might be confirmed in faith and might afford an example to others.

*While he was yet,* etc. ((BEDA.)) The woman being healed, straightway the girl is announced dead: because the Church of the Gentiles, cured of the stain of vices, and for the merit of her faith, etc., *as far as* but what is impossible to men is possible to God.

*To the ruler of the synagogue.* The ruler of the synagogue is the company of the teachers of the law, of whom: *Upon the chair of Moses have sitten the scribes and the Pharisees ((Matth. XXVIII))*. And if they shall be willing to believe, the Synagogue also that is subject to them shall be saved.

*And he admitted not,* etc. ((BEDA.)) The mysteries are not to be revealed to blasphemers and mockers, but to the faithful who may honour them. Whence elsewhere: *Wisdom is justified by all her children ((Matth. XI))*.

*Weeping and wailing. (ID)*. *Let all rejoice that hope in the Lord, and they shall exult for ever, and thou shalt dwell in them ((Psal. V))*. This gladness the Synagogue lost by the desert of her unbelief: and therefore she lies dead among those that weep and howl. But Jesus does not suffer her to perish utterly.

*She is not dead.* To me, in whose disposing both the soul that has been received lives and the flesh that is to be raised rests. Hence it is a custom among Christians that the dead, who are not doubted to be about to rise again, are called sleepers; whence: *We will not have you ignorant, brethren, concerning them that sleep ((I Thess. IV))*.

((BEDA.)) Since the soul that shall have sinned dies, yet that soul which the Lord foresees unto eternal life may not unfittingly be said to have been dead indeed to us, but to have fallen asleep to him.

*All being cast out. ((ID.))* The crowd is cast out that the girl may be raised: because unless the multitude of secular cares be cast out from the heart, the soul that lies dead within is not raised. For while it scatters itself through all its thoughts, it in no wise gathers itself to the consideration of itself.

*Talitha cumi.* In the Syriac speech which the evangelist sets down it is no more than: Girl, arise. But perhaps to express the force of the Lord's command he added this: *I say to thee, arise,* and took care to convey the sense of the speaker rather than his words. So often the apostles and the evangelists, when they take up some testimony, set down the sense rather than the words.

((HIER.)) To the girl it is said *Talitha cumi,* that is, Girl, arise. To the ruler of the synagogue, etc., *as far as* whence it is said: *Abraham believed God, and it was reputed to him unto justice ((Jac. II))*.

((BEDA.)) That Christ raised three dead persons signifies three kinds of souls. He raises the girl, etc., *as far as* he heard of a fourth dead man when a disciple announced it: but because living men to pray for him were wanting: *Let,* he says, *the dead bury their dead ((Matth. VIII))*.

echoes.text: If a poor man, one of your brothers, is with you within any of your gates in your land which Yahweh your God gives you, you shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand from your poor brother; but you shall surely open your hand to him, and shall surely lend him sufficient for his need, which he lacks. Beware that there not be a base thought in your heart, saying, “The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand”; and your eye be evil against your […]
echoes.note: Paul's appeal that the Macedonians gave generously out of deep poverty rests on the Deuteronomic open-hand command: do not harden your heart against the poor brother but give freely. The 'fellowship in service to the saints' (v.4) reflects the same covenantal obligation to relieve a needy member of God's people. Coherence with the whole collection theme is high, though the verbal link is thematic rather than lexical.

echoes.text: There is one who scatters, and increases yet more. There is one who withholds more than is appropriate, but gains poverty. The liberal soul shall be made fat. He who waters shall be watered also himself.
echoes.note: The paradox that the Macedonians' deep poverty 'abounded to the riches of their liberality' (v.2) echoes the wisdom maxim that one who scatters yet increases and the liberal soul is made rich. The generosity-brings-abundance reversal is a recurring sapiential theme Paul draws on through the chapter; volume is modest, coherence strong.

echoes.text: ‘Take from among you an offering to Yahweh. Whoever is of a willing heart, let him bring it, Yahweh’s offering: gold, silver, brass,
echoes.note: The Macedonians giving 'of their own accord' and begging to share in the collection (vv.3-4) recalls the willing-hearted offering for the tabernacle, where everyone whose heart stirred him brought a freewill gift. The collection-for-the-sanctuary typology underlies Paul's framing of the Jerusalem fund as a sacred offering. Faint and contested as a deliberate echo.

echoes.text: He who has a generous eye will be blessed; for he shares his food with the poor.
echoes.note: The summons to a willing readiness in giving 'according to what you have' (vv.11-12) resonates with the blessing on the bountiful eye that gives bread to the poor. The wisdom tradition that values the disposition of the giver over the amount stands behind Paul's stress on willingness; the link is thematic and faint.

echoes.text: For he grew up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of dry ground. He has no good looks or majesty. When we see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him. He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him. Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and […]
echoes.note: The Christological reversal in v.9, 'though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor,' may evoke the Servant who, despised and stripped of form, is poured out and yet by his abasement enriches the many. The pattern of voluntary self-impoverishment for others' gain coheres with Isaiah's Servant, but the conceptual frame of pre-existent riches is Pauline rather than verbal Isaianic; contested.

echoes.text: When they measured it with an omer, he who gathered much had nothing over, and he who gathered little had no lack. They gathered every man according to his eating.
echoes.note: Verse 15 explicitly quotes ('as it is written') the manna narrative: 'He who gathered much had nothing left over, and he who gathered little had no lack.' Paul lifts the LXX wording of the equalizing of the manna to ground his principle of economic equality among the assemblies. Volume, explicit citation formula, and coherence with the equality theme are all maximal.

echoes.text: “‘If your brother has become poor, and his hand can’t support himself among you; then you shall uphold him. He shall live with you like an alien and a temporary resident. Take no interest from him or profit, but fear your God; that your brother may live among you. You shall not lend him your money at interest, nor give him your food for profit.
echoes.note: The principle of 'equality' so that one's abundance supplies another's lack (vv.13-14) resonates with the Jubilee/sabbatical ethic of sustaining the impoverished brother without profit. The leveling vision behind Paul's mutual-supply argument is at home in the Holiness Code's economy of need; faint and thematic.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: “‘If a woman has a discharge of her blood many days not in the time of her period, or if she has a discharge beyond the time of her period; all the days of the discharge of her uncleanness shall be as in the days of her period: she is unclean. Every bed whereon she lies all the days of her discharge shall be to her as the bed of her period: and everything whereon she sits shall be unclean, as the uncleanness of her period. Whoever touches these things […]
echoes.note: The woman 'with an issue of blood' (v.25) embodies the Levitical zavah: a woman with a discharge beyond her period is unclean all the days of the flow, and whatever and whoever she touches becomes unclean. Her touching Jesus' garment (v.27) inverts the expected contagion — purity flows outward rather than impurity inward. Very high Volume and Thematic Coherence; the legal background is essential to the scene's meaning.

echoes.text: “‘If a woman has a discharge, and her discharge in her flesh is blood, she shall be in her impurity seven days: and whoever touches her shall be unclean until the evening.
echoes.note: The baseline menstrual-impurity law ('seven days she shall be in her impurity, and whoever touches her shall be unclean') frames the chronic twelve-year condition (v.25). Establishes that the woman is perpetually outside normal social and cultic contact, deepening the audacity of her approach in the crowd.

echoes.text: The priest shall offer the one for a sin offering, and the other for a burnt offering; and the priest shall make atonement for her before Yahweh for the uncleanness of her discharge.
echoes.note: The law's resolution requires the priest to make atonement 'for her unclean discharge,' after which she is clean. Jesus' word 'be cured of your disease' (v.34) functions as the priestly declaration of restored cleanness, the discharge being 'dried up' (v.29). Thematic coherence: Jesus enacts the role the Levitical system assigns to atonement and priestly verdict.

echoes.text: But to you who fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in its wings. You will go out, and leap like calves of the stall.
echoes.note: 'The sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings (kanaph)' — the same term denotes the hem/corner of a garment. The woman seeks healing by touching the edge of Jesus' clothes (vv.27-28), and Matthew/Luke specify the kraspedon (tassel). Faint but evocative: healing located in the garment's edge resonates with Malachi's healing 'in the wings.'

echoes.text: “Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them that they should make themselves fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations, and that they put on the fringe of each border a cord of blue: and it shall be to you for a fringe, that you may look on it, and remember all the commandments of Yahweh, and do them; and that you not follow after your own heart and your own eyes, after which you use to play the prostitute;
echoes.note: The command to wear tassels on the corners of garments as reminders of the commandments stands behind the Synoptic detail of touching the hem (here generalized as 'his clothes,' v.27). The healing power located in the garment's fringe gains resonance from the sanctity Torah attaches to the tassel; faint in Mark, who omits the tassel itself.

echoes.text: As they were burying a man, behold, they saw a band of raiders; and they threw the man into Elisha’s tomb. As soon as the man touched the bones of Elisha, he revived, and stood up on his feet.
echoes.note: Contact with Elisha's bones revives a corpse — power transmitted by touch from a holy person even involuntarily. The woman's cure by touching Jesus' garment, with power 'gone out from him' (v.30), echoes the prophetic motif of healing virtue conveyed through physical contact. Thematic, supporting the Elijah-Elisha typology that pervades the chapter.

echoes.text: After these things, the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, fell sick; and his sickness was so severe, that there was no breath left in him. She said to Elijah, “What have I to do with you, you man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to memory, and to kill my son!” He said to her, “Give me your son.” He took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into the room where he stayed, and laid him on his own bed. He cried to Yahweh, and said, […]
echoes.note: Elijah raises the widow of Zarephath's son: he goes in to where the child lies, acts privately, and 'the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived,' then Elijah presents the living child. Mark's raising of Jairus' daughter — entering where the child lay (v.40), the restoring word, the return to life (v.42) — is patterned on this paradigmatic prophetic resurrection. Strong Volume and recurrence within the chapter's Elijah-Elisha typology.

echoes.text: When Elisha had come into the house, behold, the child was dead, and laid on his bed. He went in therefore, and shut the door on them both, and prayed to Yahweh. He went up, and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the flesh of the child grew warm. Then he returned, and walked in the house once back and forth; and went up, and stretched himself on him. Then […]
echoes.note: Elisha raises the Shunammite's son: he enters alone with the dead child, shuts the door (cf. Jesus putting out the mourners, v.40), and the child revives; the mother falls at his feet (cf. Jairus, v.22). The closest single template for Jairus' daughter — privacy, exclusion of others, parental supplication, and bodily resurrection of a child — making the Elisha narrative a primary subtext.

echoes.text: He went up, and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the flesh of the child grew warm. Then he returned, and walked in the house once back and forth; and went up, and stretched himself on him. Then the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes.
echoes.note: Elisha's bodily, hands-on revival ('he put his mouth on his mouth... the flesh of the child grew warm') resonates with Jesus 'taking the child by the hand' (v.41). The motif of resurrection effected by the prophet's physical contact strengthens the Elisha typology beyond the structural parallels already noted in 4:32-37.

echoes.text: Elijah took the child, and brought him down out of the room into the house, and delivered him to his mother; and Elijah said, “Behold, your son lives.”
echoes.note: Elijah 'gave him to his mother' after the raising; Jesus likewise restores the child to her parents and orders that she be given food (v.43), confirming bodily life. The return-to-the-parent motif and the demonstration of real restored life cohere closely with the Elijah pattern.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: Jesus' euphemism 'the child is not dead, but is asleep' (v.39) trades on the OT/Second-Temple metaphor of death as sleep from which the dead awake, classically formulated in Daniel's 'many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake.' The raising functions as a proleptic sign of resurrection hope; thematic and verbal contact through the sleep-of-death idiom.

echoes.text: He said, “Swear to me,” and he swore to him. Israel bowed himself on the bed’s head.
echoes.note: Death-as-sleep language (e.g., the patriarchs 'sleeping with their fathers,' a recurrent OT idiom) underlies Jesus' 'she is asleep' (v.39), prompting the mourners' ridicule because they hear only literal sleep. Faint, depending on the broader idiom rather than a single text; cited to register the OT availability of the metaphor.

echoes.text: For his anger is but for a moment. His favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning.
echoes.note: 'Weeping may endure for a night, but joy comes in the morning' — the turning of mourning into rejoicing at a child's restoration loosely echoes the psalm's reversal from lament to deliverance, set against the 'weeping and great wailing' (v.38) Jesus overturns. Thematic only; included as a faint coherence with the chapter's reversal of death into life.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Out of the depths we cry to you, O Lord.
With you there is steadfast love and power to redeem.
A woman reaches through the crowd to touch his cloak.
If we but touch the hem, we shall be made well.
Into the room of death he speaks: Little girl, get up.
And the dead are raised; we will not fear.
Come, let us worship the God who lifts us from the deep.
We come, and we are healed. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: You have been low, lower than you say out loud, down where the morning feels like it will never come.
Out of the depths we cry to you.
A woman bleeding twelve years pushes through the crowd, certain that if she can just reach the hem of his cloak she will be whole.
Out of the depths we cry to you.
He takes a dead child by the hand and says, Talitha cum, little girl, I say to you, arise, and her breath comes back.
Out of the depths we cry to you.
So reach out here, whatever you are carrying; the same hand is stretched toward you, and morning is coming.
Out of the depths we cry to you, and you lift us up.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: From the deep places we call your name.
Out of the depths, we cry to you.
We press through the crowd to touch his cloak.
Out of the depths, we cry to you.
He takes the child's hand: Little one, arise.
Out of the depths, we cry to you.
Come, let us worship the God who raises us.
Out of the depths, we cry to you. Amen.
